turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Hello, come on in. I know this was booked as a routine review — how's life been treating you?
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Um, busy, and I've been a bit of a worrier, if I'm honest. The garden's been a nightmare with the slugs, which is neither here nor there. But I nearly didn't come.
[SEG0003] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'm glad you did. What's made you think about not coming?
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): I stopped my cholesterol tablet. I read something online and I panicked. You're not going to be cross, are you?
[SEG0005] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'm not cross. Tell me in your own words what you read, and which tablet you stopped.

[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): It was the cholesterol one, atorvastatin, the one I took once a day. Someone on a forum said twenty milligrams was enough to wreck your muscles — no, hang on, I wasn't on twenty. Mine was forty milligrams.
[SEG0007] person_1 (DOCTOR): Forty milligrams of atorvastatin. And when did you actually stop taking it?
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): Three weeks back. Well, actually, no, it was six weeks, because it was the week of my sister's birthday and I remember hiding the box.
[SEG0009] person_1 (DOCTOR): Six weeks, noted. What was it in that article that frightened you most?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): Muscles melting, liver damage, and then diabetes. My husband already has diabetes and I thought, that's me next. Is any of that even true?
[SEG0011] person_1 (DOCTOR): Bits are exaggerated and bits are worth knowing about. Serious muscle injury is rare. Have you had any muscle pain or weakness?

[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): My thighs ache a bit, heavy, like I've been climbing stairs. I can't tell you when it started, though. Days blur. Is that the statin still in me, and how long does it stay in your body?
[SEG0013] person_1 (DOCTOR): A few days at most, so six weeks later it shouldn't still be sitting in the muscle. Any trouble getting out of a chair, or very dark urine?
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): No. I can get out of a chair, and my urine's a normal colour. Should I be photographing it or something? I saw someone say that online.
[SEG0015] person_1 (DOCTOR): Please don't. Just ring us if it goes cola-coloured or the legs suddenly won't hold you. Are you still on the blood pressure tablet?
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes. Ramipril. Only every other day, though, not every day. The same forum said it can drop you through the floor.
[SEG0017] person_1 (DOCTOR): What strength is the ramipril?
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): Two point five milligrams. No — sorry — I'm getting muddled. Mine, the ramipril for my blood pressure, is five milligrams. Definitely five.
[SEG0019] person_1 (DOCTOR): So five milligrams, and it was meant to be once a day?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes, once every morning. I've been doing every other morning for a couple of months. Is that enough to cause a stroke? Have I ruined it?
[SEG0021] person_1 (DOCTOR): It can leave the pressure a bit higher, which isn't what we want, but you haven't ruined anything. Any dizziness when you take it?
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): Not really dizzy. I go a bit woozy if I stand up too fast, then it passes. Is woozy a mini-stroke? I need you to say no if it's no.
[SEG0023] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'll say no — brief wooziness on standing is not a mini-stroke. Any chest pain, or feeling short of breath?
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): No chest pain. And I'm not short of breath, even on the hill up to the chemist. I time myself, which is probably daft.
[SEG0025] person_1 (DOCTOR): Not daft, just anxious, and those answers are reassuring. You mentioned your husband and diabetes — what is it he actually takes?

[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): Metformin. Five hundred milligrams, twice a day, I think — his, not mine. They're in a dosette by the fridge. Could I just take his if statins are so awful, would metformin sort the cholesterol?
[SEG0027] person_1 (DOCTOR): No. Metformin is for his diabetes, it isn't a cholesterol treatment, and you mustn't take his supply. Have you ever been told you have diabetes yourself?

[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): No, never. They said my sugar was fine whenever they've checked. But the article said statins cause diabetes, so if I restart am I choosing a heart attack or choosing diabetes?

[SEG0029] person_1 (DOCTOR): I hear you. A statin can nudge the sugar up slightly in some people, but it does not mean you will develop diabetes, and stopping it isn't a free pass either. How long have you had the high blood pressure?

[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): Oh, ten years easy. No, wait, I'm talking nonsense — it's five-ish years, around when I retired at sixty. The cholesterol showed up a bit after that. Does five years mean the damage is already done?
[SEG0031] person_1 (DOCTOR): Five-ish years of blood pressure we can still look after. It doesn't mean the damage is done. Do you smoke at all?

[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): Never. Can't stand it. I have a glass of wine on a Saturday, sometimes a Sunday if there's a film on. Is that going to clash with the ramipril, and what about grapefruit — I had half a one yesterday, have I poisoned myself?

[SEG0033] person_1 (DOCTOR): A glass of wine at the weekend is fine with ramipril. Grapefruit matters with some statins, not with ramipril, and half a grapefruit yesterday will not have poisoned you while you're off the statin. What sort of readings have you been getting at home?

[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): This morning, before breakfast, one hundred and forty-six over ninety-two. I wrote it down so I wouldn't round it. Yesterday was more like one-thirty-something over eighty, I didn't write that one. Is one forty-six an emergency, do I need A and E?

[SEG0035] person_1 (DOCTOR): Not A and E. One forty-six over ninety-two is up a little, not an emergency. Let me take it now — that's one hundred and thirty-four over eighty-two, and your pulse is seventy-two, nice and steady.

[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): So my machine's lying? It's ancient, my daughter got it off the internet. Should I bin it? And if the clinic one is fine, why do I still have to take the tablet every single day?

[SEG0037] person_1 (DOCTOR): I wouldn't bin it yet. We can compare it properly another time. The clinic reading is better, and daily ramipril is what keeps it there — the every-other-day habit is why the home figure creeps up. Any headaches, or are the ankles swelling?
[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): No headaches. My ankles get a bit puffy by the evening, left worse than right, then they're all right by morning. That's heart failure, isn't it? Be straight with me.

[SEG0039] person_1 (DOCTOR): With no breathlessness, evening puffiness is much more often just fluid from being on your feet, not heart failure. Looking at them now, sitting here, they're not swollen. When were the last blood tests?

[SEG0040] person_2 (PATIENT): Before I stopped the atorvastatin, so longer than six weeks. I can't pin the date, I'm sorry. Were the results awful? I never open the letters — my husband reads his and I ignore mine.

[SEG0041] person_1 (DOCTOR): I haven't got those results on the screen today, so I won't invent them. My first instinct was to restart the atorvastatin today, forty milligrams, once a day, same as you were on.
[SEG0042] person_2 (PATIENT): Today? I don't think I can. What if the thigh ache was a warning? Do I take it morning or night, and is it forever, and what if I react?

[SEG0043] person_1 (DOCTOR): It would be the same forty milligram tablet, once daily, and yes it tends to be long term. But you're telling me you wouldn't trust it enough to swallow it, and the bloods are stale.
[SEG0044] person_2 (PATIENT): I wouldn't. I'd just hide them in a drawer again. Is there a test that says whether I'm one of the people who gets the muscle thing? Can we do that before any tablet?
[SEG0045] person_1 (DOCTOR): There isn't a perfect test for that, but bloods tell us where we are. I was going to start the statin this morning — actually, scratch that. We won't restart it today.

[SEG0046] person_2 (PATIENT): Oh, thank goodness. So what happens instead? I can't do a Thursday morning, that's my swimming — well, I say swimming, I mostly float. Is it two weeks? I thought you were about to say a fortnight.
[SEG0047] person_1 (DOCTOR): I did nearly say a fortnight. A month is better, so everything's back and we can actually decide. We'll revisit the statin then, not before.
[SEG0048] person_2 (PATIENT): A month. Right. Am I going to drop dead of a heart attack in that month without the tablet? I need a proper answer, not a pat on the head.

[SEG0049] person_1 (DOCTOR): You are very unlikely to have a heart attack simply from another month off it. I still want the question settled properly, not ignored. I'll book fasting lipids, liver function, kidney function because of the ramipril, and a glucose so we can park the diabetes worry.
[SEG0050] person_2 (PATIENT): Fasting means no breakfast, yes? From when, and can I have water? The kidney test — is that because I skipped days, have I damaged them by doing every other day?

[SEG0051] person_1 (DOCTOR): Water is fine, nothing else from midnight, and the test in the morning. The kidney check is routine on ramipril, not because I think you've damaged them. Please go back to five milligrams every morning, not every other day.
[SEG0052] person_2 (PATIENT): Every morning, even if the home reading looks all right? What if it goes too low and I faint in the kitchen? What number should make me stop and ring you?
[SEG0053] person_1 (DOCTOR): Don't stop it yourself if you feel well. If you feel faint, or the top number is under a hundred, ring us that day rather than waiting. Otherwise carry on daily.

[SEG0054] person_2 (PATIENT): Under a hundred, top number. All right. And I'm not allergic to medicines, as far as I know — nobody's ever said I was. Does that change the statin, because some people are allergic, aren't they?
[SEG0055] person_1 (DOCTOR): No allergy history doesn't push us towards a different drug. Anything else you take — vitamins, ibuprofen, anything borrowed?

[SEG0056] person_2 (PATIENT): No vitamins. I took ibuprofen for a headache last winter, but not for ages. Nothing borrowed. I promise I won't touch his metformin. Is ibuprofen a problem with ramipril, if my thighs play up?

[SEG0057] person_1 (DOCTOR): Occasional ibuprofen isn't ideal alongside ramipril, so if the thighs ache, paracetamol is kinder. You don't need ibuprofen for this. And his metformin stays in his dosette.

[SEG0058] person_2 (PATIENT): Paracetamol, not ibuprofen. How many? I always forget if it's two. And the blood tests — will it hurt, and do I get the results by post or do I have to wait the whole month in the dark?

[SEG0059] person_1 (DOCTOR): Two five-hundred-milligram tablets of paracetamol, up to four times a day if you need them, and don't go over that. I'll go through the blood results with you at the month review, rather than leaving you to a letter.

[SEG0060] person_2 (PATIENT): Two tablets, four times at most, not ibuprofen. And I still don't start the cholesterol one. What if the blood tests come back terrible — will you ring me sooner than a month, or do I just sit with it?

[SEG0061] person_1 (DOCTOR): If something needs acting on sooner, we'll ring you. Otherwise I'll see you in a month and we'll decide together whether the statin goes back, and at what dose. No restart before that.
[SEG0062] person_2 (PATIENT): Decide together. All right. Can I ask one more daft thing? If the cholesterol is normal off the tablet, can I stay off it for good? I really don't want to go back on it.

[SEG0063] person_1 (DOCTOR): You can ask that, and it's not daft. If the result is genuinely fine we might leave it, but if it's up I'd still recommend restarting. We make that call with the numbers, in a month, not today.

[SEG0064] person_2 (PATIENT): OK. I think my brain's full. So, every day for the ramipril, nothing of his, fast from midnight, bloods, then back in a month, and if my wee goes dark or I can't stand I ring. Did I miss anything?
[SEG0065] person_1 (DOCTOR): That's the lot. And if you get chest pain that doesn't settle, don't wait for me — call for help the same day. You've done the right thing telling me all this.
[SEG0066] person_2 (PATIENT): I was sure you'd shout. Thank you for not. I'll try not to read the forum at midnight. See you in a month, then, unless you ring.

spec.situation: Patient on routine review who admits stopping the cholesterol tablet after reading something online, still takes the BP tablet but 'every other day'; mentions husband's diabetes pills; doctor does not scold, plans repeat blood tests and revisits the statin decision in a month.
features: self_correction: a speaker states a number, drug name or duration and then corrects it in the same turn or later ('seventy-five... no, hundred and fifty'). The label holds only the corrected value.
doctor_changes_mind: the doctor says one plan, then changes it after new information; the label holds the final plan.

third_party_medicine: someone mentions a medicine or condition that belongs to a relative or friend (the sister's biotin, the husband's metformin). It must not appear as the patient's own; a relative's illness can only be family history if said as such.

spoken_numbers: doses, vitals and durations are spoken as words or sloppy speech ('a hundred and two point five', 'one-forty over ninety', 'five-ish years', 'twenty milligram'); the label writes them normally (102.5, 140/90, 20 mg) and does not turn vague ones into exact ones.

bad.reason: Husband's diabetes is mentioned, but this is not family history.
Ibuprofen for headache is supported, but 'discontinued' is too strong; she said not for ages.
Earlier contact is conditional, but transcript says staff will ring, not a consultation.
bad.text: Follow-up consultation (action_type=follow_up, status=conditional, responsible_person=doctor, time_reference=value: if something needs acting on sooner)

bad.reason: If results need action sooner, they will ring; not explicitly a consultation.
bad.text: consultation (time_reference=value: if something needs acting on sooner, status=conditional)

omissions.text: Ramipril is recorded incorrectly as every other morning; the patient said the prescribed regimen was 5 mg once every morning, but she has only been taking it every other morning for a couple of months.
Negative finding: no muscle weakness was reported when asked ('Have you had any muscle pain or weakness?'); only thigh aching was present.
Negative finding: no dizziness with ramipril, only brief wooziness when standing up too fast that passes.
Negative finding: not short of breath even on the hill up to the chemist.
Home blood pressure trend detail omitted: yesterday's reading was 'one-thirty-something over eighty' though not written down.
Doctor stated previous blood test results were not available on the screen that day and were therefore not reviewed.

Initial plan/discussion omitted: the doctor first intended to restart atorvastatin 40 mg once daily that day, then changed the plan and decided not to restart it today because the patient would not take it and the bloods were stale.
Real disagreement/hesitancy omitted: the patient explicitly said she could not restart atorvastatin today and would not trust herself to swallow it, and would just hide the tablets again.
Follow-up purpose detail omitted: at the 1-month review they will decide together whether to restart the statin and at what dose.

omissions.text: Ramipril is recorded as 'currently used' once every morning, but the patient said she has actually been taking 5 mg every other morning for a couple of months rather than daily.
Patient-reported home blood pressure from the previous day was approximately 'one-thirty-something over eighty' in addition to the recorded 146/92 this morning.

No muscle weakness was elicited: when asked about 'muscle pain or weakness', the patient reported thigh aching but denied trouble getting out of a chair, which supports absence of significant weakness.
The patient denied shortness of breath specifically even on exertion, saying she was not short of breath 'even on the hill up to the chemist.'
Negative finding not recorded: patient denied smoking ever and said she 'can't stand it' (stronger wording but same fact already captured).

Medicine history detail missing: husband's metformin was identified as 500 mg twice a day, and explicitly noted to be his not hers.
Investigation timing detail missing: fasting bloods were to be done in the morning, with water allowed and nothing else from midnight.
Follow-up scheduling detail missing: doctor initially nearly suggested a fortnight but decided a month was better so everything would be back before deciding about the statin.
